title: Mutual fund charges: what you pay, including the easy-to-miss ones
summary: Every charge on a mutual fund in one list: expense ratio, exit load, stamp duty, STT and GST, with when each is taken and who receives it.
body_markdown:
## What charges do you pay on a mutual fund?


You pay a yearly fee called the expense ratio, an exit load if you sell early, and two small taxes on transactions. The taxes are stamp duty, when new units are issued to you, and STT, when you redeem equity-oriented fund units. STT is securities transaction tax, and redeeming means selling units back to the fund. Tax on any gain is separate, and you pay it when you file your return.


An equity-oriented fund is one with at least 65% of its money in shares of Indian listed companies.


SEBI's rules allow only these to be charged to you as an investor in a mutual fund: the expense ratio, brokerage and trading costs, government levies and taxes, and an exit load if the fund has one. The rule says "levies as may be specified by the Board", so SEBI can add a levy later. It does not govern what a bank or a platform charges its own customer under its own terms.


Here is the whole list in one place. The NAV is the price of one unit of the fund.


Charge When it is taken Where you see it Who receives it


Expense ratio A little every day, as a yearly percentage Inside the NAV, so never as a bill The scheme's costs, including the fund house's fee


Brokerage, exchange and clearing charges As the fund trades Counted in the expense ratio Paid out of the scheme's assets


Exit load Only if you sell within the scheme's period Deducted from your payout Credited to the scheme, after GST


Stamp duty Once on each issue of units: 0.005% Slightly fewer units allotted State government


STT Once on redeeming equity-oriented fund units: 0.001% Deducted from your payout Central government


GST Inside the expense ratio, and out of any exit load Not as a separate line on a purchase or a sale Government


Tax on gains When you file your return Your capital gains statement Government


The expense ratio, with the trading costs and GST counted inside it, is taken every day as a yearly percentage. Stamp duty, STT and any exit load come once, on a purchase or a sale. Tax on gains is paid when you file your return.


## Are there hidden charges in mutual funds?


No charge is secret, but the biggest one is easy to miss because it never arrives as a bill. The expense ratio is taken inside the NAV, so the fee is already out of the price you see.


Each charge is written down somewhere you can check.


- **Expense ratio:** fund houses must show each scheme's total expense ratio every day on their own website and on AMFI's website. AMFI is the Association of Mutual Funds in India. The scheme information document, the fund's offer document, links to the last six months of daily figures.
- **Exit load:** it sits in the "Load Structure" row at the front of the scheme information document. If a scheme changes its load, the latest structure must be attached to the document. Your account statements continue to include the load structure.
- **Fee changes:** you get at least three working days' notice by email or SMS before the base expense ratio (the part SEBI caps) changes. There is no notice when the change follows from the fund's size or is a cut that regulation requires.


You will find the documents themselves on our[scheme documents page](https://koshex.com/scheme-related-documents) .


## What is the expense ratio, and when is it taken?


The expense ratio is the fund's yearly fee, shown as a percentage of your money and taken out of the fund's value a little every day. The fee is counted as a cost of the fund every day, before that day's NAV is worked out. It comes out in a falling market as well as a rising one. The NAV you see, and every return quoted from it, already has the fee taken out.


The figure SEBI asks funds to publish is the total expense ratio. It adds up the base expense ratio, brokerage, transaction costs on trades and statutory levies, including GST (Goods and Services Tax). For an open-ended index fund or ETF, the maximum base expense ratio is 0.90% of daily net assets, which is what the fund holds, less what it owes, each day.


An index fund is a fund that follows an index such as the NIFTY 50. An ETF, or exchange traded fund, is a mutual fund that tracks an index or a metal and trades on a stock exchange. Open-ended means the fund has no end date, so you can put money in or take it out when you choose.


How the ratio is built, and what each part pays for, is in our guide to the[expense ratio](https://koshex.com/blog/what-is-expense-ratio-and-why-is-it-important) . Where the fund house's share goes is in[how mutual fund companies make money](https://koshex.com/blog/how-mutual-fund-companies-make-money) .


## What do you pay when you buy units?


There is no entry load on any mutual fund scheme. You buy at the NAV that applies to your order, and the only charge that comes off at purchase is stamp duty.


Stamp duty is a small tax the state charges when new units are issued to you: 0.005% of the amount, about ₹5 on ₹1 lakh. SEBI's own example is units worth ₹1 crore, which attract ₹500. It is worked out on the value of the units, not on any other charge.


It applies each time new units are issued to you:


- every lumpsum purchase (one larger payment)
- each SIP instalment (a SIP invests a fixed amount at regular intervals)
- a[switch](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-switch-mutual-fund-schemes) into a fund (a sale in one scheme and a purchase in another of the same fund house)
- reinvested IDCW, which are payouts the fund would otherwise have made to you


It is taken by giving you slightly fewer units, so there is no separate debit. Take a ₹1,00,000 purchase in an equity-oriented fund at an assumed NAV of ₹40. Before stamp duty that is 2,500 units. After about ₹5 of duty you are allotted 2,499.875 units.


There is no stamp duty when you redeem. SEBI's FAQ on stamp duty says redemption is neither a transfer nor an issue nor a sale. A gift of units with no payment involved does not attract it either.


Fund houses used to be allowed to pay a transaction charge out of larger investments. SEBI scrapped it on 8 August 2025, and no such charge applies to a purchase or a SIP today.


## What do you pay when you sell units?


Selling can cost you an exit load, STT on equity-oriented fund units, and tax on any gain. Redeeming means selling units back to the fund. You are paid the NAV that applies, less any exit load.


An exit load is a fee some funds charge if you sell within a set time after buying. The law says an open-ended scheme cannot charge more than 3% of NAV. Each scheme sets its own period and rate.[Liquid funds](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories/liquid-funds) are the exception: they must charge a load on exits within 7 calendar days, on a graded scale set by AMFI with SEBI. The money is credited to the scheme. Our article on the[exit load](https://koshex.com/blog/exit-load-in-mutual-funds) shows how it is worked out, including on a SIP.


STT is a small tax taken when you sell equity-oriented fund units. When you redeem them with the fund, 0.001% of the amount is deducted: ₹1.50 on ₹1.5 lakh. It is paid by the seller, and nothing is charged on the buying side. SBI Mutual Fund's statement of additional information is a document the fund house publishes. It puts it this way: STT applies only to the sale or redemption of units of equity-oriented funds.


Tax on your gain is a separate matter, and it is not charged by the fund. No tax is deducted at source when a resident investor redeems, so you work it out and pay when you file. The rates depend on the type of fund and how long you held it. They are set out in[how SIP returns are taxed](https://koshex.com/blog/how-sip-returns-are-taxed) , and the figures for your own sales are in your[capital gains statement](https://koshex.com/capital-gains-statement) .


Here is a sale, with assumed numbers. Suppose an equity-oriented fund was bought three years ago and the holding is now worth ₹1,50,000. Assume the exit-load period is over, so there is no load. STT of ₹1.50 comes off the payout. The expense ratio was never a separate deduction, because the ₹1,50,000 is already after it. Redemption proceeds must reach you within 3 working days. For schemes that put at least 80% into permitted overseas investments, the limit is 5 working days. For the steps, see[how to sell mutual funds online](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-sell-mutual-funds-online-a-step-by-step-guide) .


## Is GST charged on mutual funds?


GST is already counted inside the expense ratio. If an exit load is charged, the GST on it is paid out of the load before the rest goes back to the fund. SEBI's rule says the exit load, net of GST, is credited to the scheme.


So GST reaches you in those two places and not as a separate line on a purchase or a sale. Tax on your gains is income tax, not GST.


## Do apps, banks or Koshex charge anything extra?


Charges of a platform or a bank come from that platform or bank, not from the scheme. They are set out in its own terms. Koshex charges investors no platform or transaction fee. The expense ratio and any exit load are different. They are the scheme's costs, set by the scheme and shown in its documents, and they apply however you invest. Stamp duty, STT and tax on your gains apply in the same way.


Your bank may charge a fee when a SIP debit fails. A mandate is the bank permission behind SIP debits, and SBI's schedule of charges, updated 30 September 2025, lists ₹250 plus GST for a failed one. Charges differ from bank to bank, so look at your own bank's list. We cover mandates in[one-time mandate for a SIP](https://koshex.com/blog/one-time-mandate-otm-sip) .


You do not need a demat account (an account that holds units in electronic form) to hold mutual fund units. It is needed only if you want to trade units on a stock exchange. Your money also goes straight from your bank account into the scheme, with no pooling on the way.


To see the schemes themselves, start from our[mutual funds page](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds) .
